title: Riders went up a California mountain by steam and came down with no engine

cover.alt: Black-and-white film still from 1917: a single railway track runs down a steep, scrubby hillside, with open cars full of passengers coming down it.

body: From 1896, steam locomotives hauled tourists up the **Mount Tamalpais** railway north of San Francisco, billed as the “Crookedest Railroad in the World”: in 8.19 miles it wound its way about 2,366 feet up the mountain. From 1902 riders could come back down in open **gravity cars**, which simply coasted down the track. A “gravityman” controlled the speed with two brake levers, under a limit of 12 mph. Once cars could drive to the summit, riders dwindled, and the last train ran in October 1929.

slides.alt: Black-and-white film: the view from a car full of passengers in hats as it coasts round a mountainside curve, then open cars marked Mt Tamalpais Gravity roll down a steep slope past the camera while the riders wave.
slides.caption: 1917: riding down in a gravity car, then cars marked “Mt Tamalpais Gravity” coast down the slope past the camera as the riders wave.

slides.question: In 1898, Scientific American counted the curves on the 8.19-mile main line. How many?
slides.explanation: 266 curves, leaving only about 3.3 miles of straight track on the whole main line.

slides.heading: Up the mountain
slides.note: Grades averaged 5%, and reached 7% in places.

slides.question: What finally killed the railway?
options: Cars could drive to the summit
slides.explanation: Riders dwindled once the automobile could reach the top. A wildfire in July 1929 burned nearly 100 homes nearby, and the line was dismantled in 1930.
